name: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)

what.text: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a hormone made by the placenta in pregnancy. It is a glycoprotein with two parts, an alpha and a beta subunit. The FDA-approved products, Novarel and Pregnyl, are purified from the urine of pregnant women.
How it acts, according to the FDA labels:

items.text: Its action is almost the same as luteinizing hormone (LH) from the pituitary gland, with a small amount of FSH-like activity.
In men it stimulates the Leydig cells of the testes to make androgens, including testosterone.
In boys it may help an undescended testis move down when nothing is physically blocking it. This is often temporary.
The labels state that hCG has no known effect on fat mobilization, appetite, hunger or body fat distribution.

research.text: hCG is approved for a few specific uses. Its use alongside testosterone to keep up testicular function or sperm production is off-label. The human studies of that use that we found are small: a 3-week randomized study in 29 healthy men and a review of 26 patients’ records. Each is listed below as it was run.

research.title: Low-dose hCG and testicular testosterone, 2005 (USA)

facts.v: randomized, with a saline placebo group
29 healthy men with normal reproductive function
weekly testosterone enanthate injections, plus either saline or one of three low doses of hCG every other day
testosterone inside the testis, sampled by fine-needle aspiration

research.found: Testosterone alone cut testosterone inside the testis by 94%. Adding hCG raised it in step with the dose. The study did not measure sperm production or fertility.

src.label: Coviello et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2005

research.title: hCG with testosterone therapy, 2013 (USA)

facts.v: retrospective review of records. No control group, no placebo.
26 men with low testosterone, mean age 35.9; 19 on testosterone injections and 7 on gel, all also on low-dose hCG
hormone levels, semen tests and pregnancies

research.found: No differences in semen measures were seen during follow-up, and no man stopped producing sperm. Nine of the 26 men fathered a pregnancy with their partner. Without a control group, the study cannot show what would have happened without hCG.

research.text: What the labels say about approved uses

items.text: The labels say hCG has not been shown to be effective in treating obesity. There is no substantial evidence that it increases weight loss beyond calorie restriction, improves fat distribution, or reduces hunger on a diet.
For undescended testes, the labels say descent is permanent in some cases but temporary in most.

us.text: hCG is FDA approved, as Novarel and Pregnyl, for undescended testes in boys, selected cases of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in men, and ovulation induction in women. Since March 23, 2020 it has been regulated as a biologic. FDA says biologics are not eligible for the 503A and 503B compounding exemptions. As of October 31, 2026.

after.text: Australia’s Poisons Standard (June 2026) lists human chorionic gonadotrophin in Schedule 4 (prescription-only), except in pregnancy test kits. We could not reach the TGA’s register to confirm which products are registered.
The EU authorisation found is for Ovitrelle, which is used in women to trigger ovulation. We did not find an EU-wide authorisation of hCG for men.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Chorionic gonadotrophin (CG) is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition) in males under class S2.2.1, testosterone-stimulating peptides, on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List. It is a non-Specified Substance. We could not open the 2027 list to check for changes.

side.text: The labels list headache, irritability, fatigue, depression, swelling, breast growth and injection-site pain, plus allergic reactions including anaphylaxis. In women, the main serious risk is ovarian hyperstimulation.

items.text: headache, irritability, restlessness, depression, fatigue, edema (swelling), precocious puberty, gynecomastia (breast growth) and pain at the injection site.

redness, hives, rash, angioedema (deep swelling of the skin) and shortness of breath have been reported. The labels say it is unclear whether these come from the hormone or the benzyl alcohol diluent. Anaphylaxis has been reported with urine-derived hCG.
there have been sporadic reports of testicular tumors in healthy young men given hCG for secondary infertility. A causal link has not been established.
the androgen rise can cause early puberty in boys treated for undescended testis.
the labels advise caution in people with heart or kidney disease, epilepsy, migraine or asthma.
hCG can interfere with blood tests for LH.

ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, which can be life-threatening, ovarian cyst enlargement or rupture, multiple births and arterial blood clots, when used with other fertility drugs. hCG may harm a fetus.
the supplied diluent contains benzyl alcohol, linked to a fatal “gasping syndrome” in premature infants.

unconfirmed: MHRA’s product register needs JavaScript and could not be read, so UK status is not confirmed.
Australia’s TGA register (tga.gov.au) could not be reached, so we could not confirm which hCG products are registered there. Only the Poisons Standard scheduling is reported.
We could not open WADA’s 2027 Prohibited List, so any 2027 change is not reported.
We did not find a large randomized trial of hCG given with testosterone therapy. Only the two studies reported were found.
surprises: The FDA labels say hCG has not been shown to help with weight loss, and FDA warns consumers to avoid hCG diet products. hCG is still widely sold for weight loss.

Since March 23, 2020, hCG is a biologic, and FDA says biologics are not eligible for the 503A and 503B compounding exemptions. FDA named hCG as affected. “Compounded hCG” is still commonly advertised.

Using hCG to keep up sperm production during testosterone therapy is off-label. The studies behind it are small: 29 men for 3 weeks (testicular testosterone only, no sperm measures) and a 26-man record review with no control group.
The labels report sporadic testicular tumors in young men given hCG for infertility (no causal link established), which is rarely mentioned in marketing.
